key_findings.finding: The primary and apparently only directly relevant rat-tail experiment located is Onishi et al., “Topical bFGF Improves Secondary Lymphedema through Lymphangiogenesis in a Rat Tail Model” (PMID 25426379, 2014). Rats received daily topical bFGF versus saline control after tail-lymphedema induction; the available abstract does not state the formulation, concentration, amount, or application area, so the intervention dose cannot be verified from the retrieved evidence.

Topical bFGF improved lymphedema-related outcomes: tail volume was lower than saline control (P<0.05), and indocyanine-green fluorescence declined earlier, interpreted as improved lymphatic drainage/function. Tissue subcutaneous and deep areas also withered more rapidly in the bFGF group, with significant differences at postoperative day 14.

The study provides convergent lymphangiogenic evidence: VEGF-C mRNA and protein were increased with bFGF at postoperative day 14 (P<0.01), and histologic lymphatic-vessel density was higher at day 14 (P<0.05). VEGF-D mRNA was also measured, but the retrieved abstract does not report a significant VEGF-D result; LYVE-1 or VEGFR-3 measurements were not identified in the retrieved text.

key_findings.finding: Overall, the evidence supports an association consistent with a lymphangiogenic mechanism rather than symptom-only improvement: functional drainage, VEGF-C induction, and increased lymphatic-vessel density changed in parallel. However, causality is not definitively established because the experiment did not, in the retrieved evidence, block FGF2/VEGF-C signaling or otherwise show that preventing lymphangiogenesis abolishes the volume/fluorescence benefit; the authors’ causal wording therefore exceeds what a mechanistic intervention test can prove.
